$comment: A LANGUAGE prior. Data only, no code. Staged here for transfer to eoPriors; nothing in packages/ may hardcode any of it.

provenance.source: English Wikipedia, 'Basque grammar', section on negation, fetched 2026-08-19 — itself drawing on the standard academic descriptions of Basque syntax (the article's own citation lineage traces to de Rijk's 'Standard Basque: A Progressive Grammar' and comparable reference grammars). Quoted directly: 'Negation is expressed by ez preceding the finite verb form.' and, for compound tenses: 'Compound tense forms of verbs, and also compound verbs, are negated by placing ez in front of the finite auxiliary (or light verb).'
provenance.built_by: hand-curated from one citable source, deliberately minimal rather than padded with recalled-but-uncited items

attested.period: Continuously attested as far back as the written record reaches, with no claimed change-point — this is the rare honest answer of 'stable across documented history' rather than a datable date range. The earliest substantial Basque prose corpora both de Rijk's grammar and the diachronic literature draw on (Etxepare 1545, Leizarraga's 1571 New Testament translation) show no different ez-to-finite-verb relationship. A genuinely DIFFERENT, adjacent fact DOES have a real dated change and must not be conflated with this one: whether the non-finite MAIN verb could precede the already-adjacent [ez+auxiliary] unit ('VP Preposing') — de Rijk states this option 'up to the end of the 19th century, many varieties of Basque retained' but is no longer grammatical 'nowadays' (citing Lardizabal 1855); Salaberri (2021) independently corpus-dates this same shift across roughly the 16th-20th centuries, progressing region-by-region (east first, west more conservative). In BOTH the older and newer orders, ez itself sits immediately before the finite auxiliary — the specific relationship this prior's `negation` entry encodes never flips, even while that adjacent fact changed.
attested.basis: de Rijk, Rudolf P.G. (2008), Standard Basque: A Progressive Grammar, Vol. 1, MIT Press — §8.2.1-8.2.4 'Syntax of Negation'/'Auxiliary Attraction' (pp.165-168) and §8.4 'Relative Order of Participle and Auxiliary' (pp.169-170, p.196 footnote on VP Preposing), read directly from the primary source (theswissbay.ch PDF mirror) rather than relying on Wikipedia's paraphrase alone. Corroborated by Salaberri, Iker (2021), 'The word order of negation in the history of Basque', Diachronica 38(2):259-301 — abstract confirmed verbatim via the Semantic Scholar API; full paper text could NOT be independently read (addi.ehu.es returned HTTP 503 throughout; ResearchGate/Academia.edu mirrors returned HTTP 403), so its specific findings rest on the verified abstract plus consistent WebSearch-engine summaries of the body, not a directly-read primary quote — flagged rather than passed off as fully verified.
attested.confidence: high for 'ez adjoins the finite verb, continuously, no claimed change-point' (grounded in a primary source read directly); medium for the specific 16th-20th-century dating of the adjacent VP-Preposing shift (abstract-plus-summary only)

region.detail: The specific fact this prior encodes (ez immediately precedes/adjoins the finite verb or auxiliary, nothing intervening) is structurally pan-dialectal, not Standard-Basque(Batua)-specific. De Rijk's grammar states 'Auxiliary Attraction' as a general Basque fact grounded in a proposed syntactic universal (Laka's Tense C-Command Condition), not flagged as standard-only; the grammar's own subject index has no dialect-specific subentry under 'Negation', and its entries for Souletin/Zuberoan (the most divergent traditional dialect), Roncalese, and Salazarese list no negation-word-order divergence — for a grammar that otherwise catalogs dozens of dialect-specific quirks per dialect entry, that absence is itself informative. Salaberri (2021) reports, per its verified abstract, that 'no correlation could be found between dialect and the word order of negation' for the variable it measured. What DOES vary by dialect is the adjacent VP-Preposing fact named in `attested` above (where the non-finite main verb sits RELATIVE TO the already-adjacent [ez+auxiliary] unit) — eastern dialects historically more innovative, western more conservative — a narrower, different fact than the one this prior's `negation` array actually encodes.
region.basis: Same primary/secondary sources as `attested` above: de Rijk (2008) §8.2 and Subject Index pp.1392, 1398 (dialect entries checked directly for absent negation-order subentries); Salaberri (2021) abstract via Semantic Scholar API. The full-paper-unread caveat above applies here too.

notes: negation: the free-standing negation particle(s) that precede a finite verb or auxiliary — the same slot perceiver/text/relations.js's NEGATION_BEFORE_VERB window already checks (before the verb, within the clause), and priors.js::NEGATION_WORDS holds for English (giver lang/en).

Consumed by perceiver/text/relations.js::discoverRelationVocab and ::extractRelations via the injected `negationWords` option (a Set) — the same seam bin/priors/lang/en.json's own abbreviations already opened on spans.js::splitSentences.

'ez' is the ONLY entry, deliberately: the source article also names negative-polarity ITEMS used in negative contexts (inor 'anybody', ezer 'anything', inon 'anywhere', inoiz 'ever', inola 'any way') — these are NOT negation markers themselves (the same distinction English 'anybody' has from 'not': a negative-polarity item can appear in some non-negative contexts too, e.g. questions and conditionals), so including them here would fabricate false negatives on ordinary affirmative material. A padded list built from recalled-but-unverified extras (e.g. 'ezta') was deliberately left out rather than guessed at — this file states only what its one citation actually supports.

STRUCTURAL NOTE, worth keeping: Basque negation fronts BEFORE the finite verb by the grammar's own word order, unlike English's postposed 'not' (does NOT want). This means the existing before-the-verb window this organ already checks for is, if anything, a MORE natural fit for Basque's own negation position than for English's — not a mechanism bent to accommodate a foreign grammar, a mechanism that happens to already match a different one.

Measured against real material: eval/asserted-crosslingual.md and eval/vendored-prior-eval.md in the-fold repo record the before/after result of injecting this file's `negation` set against Domingo Agirre's Garoa (1912, public domain, klasikoak.armiarma.eus).

Added 2026-08-19 (schema NegationPrior@2): the `attested`/`region` blocks above are the grounded answer to 'chronologically stamped, regional when possible' — and this is the one prior of the three where the honest finding is genuine stability, not a disclosed gap. Basque negation word order is structurally pan-dialectal and continuously attested with no claimed change-point, checked against a primary reference grammar (de Rijk 2008) rather than assumed from the general Wikipedia article this file's own provenance already cites. Worth keeping alongside pcm.json's and en-AAVE.json's own findings (a regional-anchor-unverified gap, and documented regional variation, respectively) as three real, different answer shapes rather than three copies of the same disclaimer.
